A cage whose purpose is *Breeder* starts out *Shared*; any other cage (an experiment cage, a *Breeding* one) starts *Personal*. Only its owner or an admin shares a cage, makes it personal or gives it to someone else; admins and animal care can still see and change every cage.

- **Everyone sees the lab's databases**, because a census with holes is not a census.

- **Personal databases** (*Just you* on their tile) are seen only by their owner and admins; a [project group's](https://biomanager.org/guide/project-groups) by its members and admins.

- **Admins** can change anything, run Lab setup, approve people, and read the audit log.

- **Animal care** (technicians, vets; a role in **Manage users**) may change any lab's animals, cages, tanks and vials, but not other people's experiments, notebook pages or settings (their own they keep like a member). A **Facility manager** also runs the racks, rooms, incubators, water systems and each database's settings, but not accounts.

- **Racks & boxes** (admins, in the account menu) says who may resize, rename or delete each rack, box and incubator, in every database — fish racks and the racks of your own databases too. One with nobody is for admins only.

When a record isn't yours, BioManager says whose it is instead of just refusing.

### Troubleshooting

#### I can't edit a record

It belongs to someone else and isn't shared: BioManager says whose it is. Ask them, or an admin.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/who-can-do-what

---

## Project groups

Share animals, stock, databases and pages among the people on a project.

Who and where: Since 1.0.3

A group is some of the lab working on one project: a layer between you and the whole lab. **More → Project groups** lists them and who is in each. An admin makes a group, names it and picks its members; a group's *leads* may add and remove members too. Someone can be in several groups.

- **Shared with a group.** Wherever you choose *Shared* or *Lab common*, your groups are offered as well: a breeder cage, a plasmid or a reagent shared with a group is its members' to edit. For a breeding tank or a lab stock vial, pick the group under **Shared with** in its dialog. Everyone in the lab still sees them.

- **A group's database.** When you make a database, **Who is it for?** offers your groups: only their members (and admins) see it, and they are told it was added. **Share with the group** on the Databases page gives one of your own to a group.

- **A group's events and to-dos.** On the calendar, **Who sees it** offers your groups: the group's members see it on their calendar (and a to-do on Home), and any of them can tick a to-do off; only its maker or an admin changes an event or deletes a to-do.

- **Notebook.** **Share** on a page offers your groups as well as people, to view or to edit; a template can be for a group (**Who can use it**).

- **The colony.** **My groups**, beside My colony, shows the mice and cages of everyone in your groups.

Deleting a group (admins) makes what was shared with it its owner's own again (a breeding tank or a stock vial the lab's, as its purpose says), and a group's databases their maker's.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/project-groups

---

## People and guests

Approve sign-ups, manage admins and accounts, offer Google, Microsoft or institution sign-in, and let guests in.

Who and where: Admins

- **Joining**: New sign-ups wait for an admin's approval in **Manage users**. Members can also sign in with Google or Microsoft, or with the institution's own account, if the server offers it, and connect it under **Settings → Sign-in methods** ([setting it up](https://biomanager.org/server#sign-in)).

- **Admins**: **Manage users** promotes and demotes admins, disables accounts and resets passwords; **Lab setup** can also make someone admin. Keep at least two.

- **Leaving**: **More → Colony overview** in the sidebar (admins) lists every cage by who manages it, idle cages and living mice without a cage; hand racks over in **Racks & boxes**, then disable the account. Their records and history stay.

- **Guests**: For someone outside the lab — a collaborator, a visitor — for a day to a month: **Guests** in the account menu (admins), who it's for and how long, **Make a code**. They open the link, enter the code, and work as a member with their own account until the pass ends or you press **End now**. On a Tailscale server, the admin can let guests in from the internet without Tailscale ([how](https://biomanager.org/server#guests)).

### Troubleshooting

#### I forgot my password

Ask an admin: **Manage users** resets it.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/people-and-guests

---

## Lab setup

Turn databases on or off, and set your lab's name, time zone and dates.

Who and where: Admins only

**More → Lab setup** in the sidebar (admins) reopens the survey at any time: switch databases on or off, rename the lab, choose the calendar and notebook, and set what members may do — create their own databases, or add ones for the whole lab. Under **Who looks after the lab**, make someone admin.

Switching a database off hides it and closes it to members, even by a saved link; its data is kept, and admins can still open it (a note says it is off).

Under **Your lab**, besides its name:

- **Time zone** — what "today" and "overdue" mean, and the times shown. Blank uses the server's (or the computer's).

- **Dates** — how dates are written in lists and messages: *Sep 26, 2026*, *26 Sep 2026* or *2026-09-26*. Date fields you type into follow your computer's language.

- **Genotyping day** — the day after birth the genotyping reminder falls on (P28 unless you change it).

### Troubleshooting

#### A database disappeared from the sidebar

An admin may have switched it off in **Lab setup**; its data is kept, and it comes back when it is switched on.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/lab-setup

---

## Phones and cage cards

Use BioManager on a phone, and print cage cards and labels that open records when scanned.

Who and where: Lab server for phones

- **Android**: Install `BioManager-Android.apk` from the [download page](https://biomanager.org/download) (allow your browser to install apps when asked), type your lab server's address once, and you're in. The **Scan** button reads cage cards.

- **iPhone and iPad**: Open the server in **Safari** and tap **Share → Add to Home Screen**. BioManager gets its own icon and opens full screen like an app; your camera scans cage cards. (Android without the app: Chrome → **⋮ → Install app**.)

- **Cage cards**: **Cages → Cage cards** prints cards sized for standard card stock — owner, purpose, where it goes (rack and position), animals with how many of each sex, genotype and a QR code. Scanning it opens that cage, ready to edit, at the rack. **Tank labels** (Zebrafish), **Labels** on a fly or worm database, and **Labels** on ticked samples, reagents or any inventory's rows do the same for tanks, vials and tubes.

- **Label printers**: **Print on** chooses a sheet of cards for any printer, or a label printer's roll: Brother QL (62 × 29, 90 × 29, 100 × 62 mm), Zebra (2 × 1, 3 × 1, 4 × 2, 4 × 2.5 in) or cryo-tube labels. It then prints one label a page, typed to fit; in the print dialog pick the label printer and that label size, margins **None**. Your choice is remembered. For tubes, **On each label** chooses what a label says (box, position, lot, owner, a column such as concentration, the day printed), remembered for each database, and **Two lines for long text** wraps a long name or place instead of cutting it. For a Zebra, **Download for Zebra (.zpl)** gives the labels in its own language; or an admin adds the Zebra's address on the lab's network once (under **Send labels straight to a Zebra**), and **Send to Zebra** prints them at once.

> Phones reach a **server** , or a desktop that shares its lab on the network ([Devices](https://biomanager.org/guide/your-data#devices)): otherwise the app on one computer is private to that computer.

*A cage opened on a phone after scanning its card*

*Printable cage cards*

### Troubleshooting

#### My phone can't reach the server

Check the address with your admin; that you're on the lab's network, VPN or Tailscale; and, if your lab uses its own certificate, that it's installed on the phone.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/phones-and-cage-cards

---

## Your data and backups

Where your data is kept, how it's backed up, and how to move it.

#### The desktop app

| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/Biomanager/` |
|---|---|
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\Biomanager\` |
| Linux | `~/.local/share/Biomanager/` |

- Your data lives outside the app, so updating or reinstalling never touches it.

- Before a new version changes the database an older one made, it copies it to `data/backups/before-upgrade-….db` in that folder, next to the database itself, `data/biomanager.db` (the last ten are kept). Every release is tested opening a lab made by each earlier release, with nothing lost.

- Back that folder up with Time Machine or File History, copying it while BioManager is closed.

> **Don't keep BioManager's data in Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive or iCloud Drive.** Syncing corrupts database files. BioManager warns you if it finds itself in one.

#### A lab server

A server backs up every night, restores the newest backup every week to prove it works, and can keep encrypted copies off-site — see [Keeping the data safe](https://biomanager.org/server#safe).

#### A copy of the lab on your computer

The desktop app can keep a copy of your lab server's whole database, so the lab's records live on more than one machine:

1. On the server: **Settings → Copies of the lab on your computers**, name the computer and **Make a key**. Copy the key; it's shown once. (Admins always may; members when Lab setup allows it.)

2. On that computer, in the desktop app: **Settings → Keep a copy of your lab server**. Enter the server's address and the key, and **Save and copy now**.

3. From then on, while the app is open, it takes a fresh copy every day, checks it, keeps the last 14 and mirrors uploaded files. The card shows when the last copy was made; on the server, the list shows every computer and how fresh its copy is. **Revoke** stops a computer (a lost laptop, say) from taking more.

The copies sit beside the app's own data, which they never touch. An admin's copy is the whole lab, and can rebuild the server if it's ever lost ([how](https://biomanager.org/server#move)): treat a computer holding one like the server itself. A member's copy holds what they can see in the app: no one's password, not other people's private notebook pages or personal databases, not the Audit log. Guests can't keep a copy.

#### One lab on many devices

One device holds the lab's **master copy**; every other one works on it through its address, so nothing is ever merged and nothing written in two places is lost. **Settings → Devices** shows which device it is, and every computer linked to the lab (by a key from **Copies of the lab**): how it uses the lab, its version, when it was last heard from.

- **A lab server** is the master copy unless an admin hands it on.

- **Open the lab in this window** (a linked desktop): the app's window opens the lab itself, as a browser would, and the computer keeps its daily copy. **Go → This Computer's BioManager** comes back to its own.

- **Share this lab on the network** (a desktop, admins): the computer becomes the master for every device on the same network, which opens the address it shows and signs in with an account there. It must stay on and awake. The connection isn't encrypted, so share only on a network you trust; for anywhere else, a lab server. Its own pages (setting up a server, its copies, its devices) are never offered to another device.

- **Make it the master** (on the master, admins): for a linked desktop with an admin's key, open now, on the same version. Within a minute it freezes the master (read only, so no change is lost), takes a last copy, keeps its own data in `backups/before-taking-over-….db`, and shares the lab on its network. The old master stays read only, with a banner pointing everyone there. Everyone signs in again with their lab account. Sign-ins to other services (Google Calendar) are not carried and are connected again.

- **Give the master copy back** (on the desktop holding it): its database and new files go back; the other device keeps what it had in `backups/before-taking-back-….db` and is the master again. The desktop turns read only and opens the lab there; **Go back to this computer's own lab** restores what it had before it took over.

- If the computer holding the master copy is lost, an admin on the old master chooses **Make this the master again**: what was changed on the lost computer since is not there.

#### Everyone

**Export** on any sheet downloads what it shows as CSV, which opens in Excel. On the Mice sheet, **Export → Excel** is a workbook that **Import from Excel** reads back. A note that starts with `=` stays text in every export, never a formula. **Export my data** (in the account menu, and in Settings) downloads your own mice, cages, weights, experiments and plasmids as CSV, each plasmid's sequence as a GenBank file with its features and the files kept with it, your notebook pages and your profile, in one zip.

#### What BioManager sends its makers

Your records never leave your computer or your lab's server. So that BioManager's makers know how many labs use it, each installation sends one short message a day, with counts only:

- the version, whether it is the desktop app or a server, the operating system and the kind of database;

- how many members, and how many changed something this week, as ranges (1, 2–5, 6–15, 16–50, 51+);

- which built-in functions are on, and how many databases of each kind;

- a random id for the installation, so a lab counts once.

Never names, email addresses, anything anyone wrote, what your databases are called, or the computer's name or address. It goes to PostHog, which is asked not to work out where it came from. Admins see exactly what is sent on the **Usage report** (**Feedback → Usage report**) and can **Switch off** there; the setup survey asks first. On a server, `BIOMANAGER_TELEMETRY=0` (or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`) in `.env` turns it off for good.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/your-data

---

## Scripts, instruments and other tools

Read and write your lab's data from scripts, R and instruments.

Who and where: Lab server or desktop

BioManager has an API: other programs can read the lab's records, and change them, as you. Pull an experiment's body weights straight into R or Python, have a balance post each weight as it weighs, let a core's system mark samples as done, or count cages for the facility — without anyone exporting a sheet.

1. **Settings → API tokens**: say what will use it (*Balance in B12*, *My R scripts*), whether it may **Read**, **Read and change** or **Read and propose** (for an AI assistant: see below), and when it ends. **Make a token**.

2. Copy the token: it is shown once. Treat it like your password, and keep it out of scripts you share (an environment variable is the usual place).

3. Send it with each request, as `Authorization: Bearer bmt_…`. The **API reference** (the link on the same card, or `/api` on your BioManager) lists everything it can read and change, with examples in curl, Python and R.

- **A token is you.** It can do what you can on the pages, no more; a change made with it is in the change history under your name, marked with the token's name.

- It can read mice, cages, litters, strains, tanks and fish, plasmids, fly and worm vials, every inventory and every experiment; and change a mouse (its cage, genotype, note, status…), record a weight, change a vial, add or change an inventory item, and record an experiment's readout.

- For a tool that starts from your own words (an AI assistant, say), it can also find the records a phrase means, each with a reference to use (`/api/v1/resolve?q=cage 88`), list what your lab calls things: strains, statuses, purposes, racks, people and each database's own fields (`/api/v1/vocabulary`), and list what is due, as Home does (`/api/v1/due`).

- Make one token for each thing that uses it, so you can **Revoke** one without the others. The card shows when each was last used. Admins see everyone's tokens and can revoke any; **Setup** can keep tokens to admins.

- With the desktop app, only programs on that computer can reach it; on a lab server, anything that can reach the server.

### Changes an assistant proposes

A token that may **Read and propose** is for an AI assistant: it changes nothing itself, and sends its changes as one proposal that you approve, whole, under **Proposed changes**. Connecting one and approving are in [AI assistants](https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants).

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/scripts-and-api

---

## AI assistants

Tell an AI assistant what you did; it proposes the records, and you approve them in BioManager.

Who and where: Lab server or desktop

BioManager has no AI inside it. If you already use an assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Cherry Studio or another app that speaks MCP), you can connect it to your lab. Tell it what you did, in your own words or with a photo of your notebook (*litter in 102 yesterday, 7 pups; moved the two old breeders from 88 to 91; injected day 3 of the TMX cohort this morning*), and it turns that into records: as one proposal, which you approve in BioManager. It never changes anything itself.

### Connect an assistant

Open **Help → Connect an AI assistant** (it is also under **Settings → API tokens**, and on an empty **Proposed changes**). It shows the ways in for your BioManager, with its address filled in. Nothing needs installing, except for Claude Desktop on the lab network (below).

#### From claude.ai, the Claude apps or ChatGPT

These apps reach BioManager from the internet, so this works when your lab's server is on the internet: its admin turns on internet access (in the server's runbook). Then the Connect page shows the **connector address**, ending in `/api/v1/mcp`. The desktop app can't be reached this way; use the way below.

1. Add BioManager as a custom connector with that address. In Claude: **Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector** (on a Team or Enterprise plan, an owner adds it first). In ChatGPT: **Settings → Connectors**, with developer mode on, then create a connector with OAuth.

2. When it asks you to connect, a BioManager page opens asking for a **connection code**. On the Connect page (on the lab network), press **Get a connection code**, type it in, and press **Allow**. A code works once, for 10 minutes.

3. That's it, on the web and in the phone app alike. The connection is listed under **Settings → API tokens** with the app's name; revoke it there to end it.

#### From Claude Code, Cursor, Cherry Studio or Claude Desktop

These run on a computer that can reach BioManager: the same computer as the desktop app, or any computer on the lab network for a lab server. No internet access is needed. You don't need to know how the connection works:

1. **Let your assistant set itself up.** On the Connect page, press **Copy the message** and send it in a chat with your coding assistant. The message has your BioManager's address in it; the assistant adds BioManager by itself, then tells you how to sign in.

2. **Sign in.** In Claude Code, type `/mcp` and choose *biomanager*. BioManager opens in your browser, asking whether to let the app connect: press **Allow**. There is no token to copy or keep.

- To do it yourself in Claude Code, the Connect page also has the one command to run in a terminal.

- For an app that can't sign in, and for **Claude Desktop**, press **Make a token**: it makes a token that may **Read and propose**, and the next page shows the setup to copy for each app. Claude Desktop runs a small program from BioManager's source, `mcp/biomanager_mcp.py`; the steps are in `mcp/README.md`.

#### Use it

Ask it: *Log today's work from my notes: …* It looks up each animal, cage and experiment you mention, asks you when something could be more than one record, and sends one proposal with a link to it.

- The assistant reads what you can read, as you. Revoke its token under **Settings → API tokens** to cut it off.

### What it can propose

- In the mouse colony, zebrafish, fly and worm databases and any other organism's: the everyday records. New animals, cages, tanks and vials; litters, weaning, moves and deaths; crosses, clutches and flips; weights and readings; scheduled jobs done.

- In an experiment: a step done, a readout, animals added, its status, a note.

- In the notebook: a line in the **Log** of today's daily log, with the time. If the page is open, the line appears in it within a few seconds.

- It can't delete anything, sign a page, or change who may see what.

- It can also tell you what is due, as Home lists it, and plan your day from it.

### Approving

A proposal tells you (the bell) and waits under **Proposed changes** in your account menu.

- Each proposal is one summary in plain words: what will change in each database, with any warnings at the top (a litter date that would be replaced, pups too young to wean). **Show each change** lists every record, before → after.

- **Approve** makes every change at once; **Discard** makes none. There is no approving one change at a time: if something is wrong, discard it and ask the assistant for a corrected proposal.

- An approved proposal is one batch in **Batch history**, marked with the assistant's name, so **Undo** takes it back whole (a line added to the notebook stays).

- If a record it touches was changed after the proposal was made, or a change no longer goes through, nothing is applied and the page says which record and why.

- Only you can approve your proposals, and only signed in to BioManager: no token can. A proposal you leave waits two weeks, then expires.

### Troubleshooting

#### The assistant says it can't reach BioManager

For Claude Code, Cursor or Cherry Studio: check that BioManager is running, that the address in the setup is its address (the desktop app's is on **Settings → API tokens**), and that the token hasn't been revoked or expired. For claude.ai, the Claude apps or ChatGPT: check that the connector address opens from a phone off the lab's Wi-Fi (it should show a short message asking for an API token), and that it ends in `/api/v1/mcp`.

#### Connecting says the connection code isn't right

A code works once and for 10 minutes. Press **Get a connection code** again and use the new one.

#### Approving says a record changed after the proposal was made

Someone (or you) changed it meanwhile, so the proposal may be out of date. **Discard** it and ask the assistant to propose again.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/ai-assistants

---

## Troubleshooting

Common problems and their fixes, each also on the page it belongs to.

- **The app won't open on my Mac**: Right-click it and choose **Open**. If macOS says it's damaged, move it to Applications first, then try again. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/install)

- **Linux: the AppImage does nothing**: Mark it executable. If it still won't start, install `libfuse2`, or use the `.tar.gz` and run `BioManager/BioManager`. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/install)

- **My phone can't reach the server**: Check the address with your admin; that you're on the lab's network, VPN or Tailscale; and, if your lab uses its own certificate, that it's installed on the phone. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/phones-and-cage-cards)

- **I can't edit a record**: It belongs to someone else and isn't shared: BioManager says whose it is. Ask them, or an admin. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/who-can-do-what)

- **A cell turned red**: That change wasn't saved; the message at the bottom says why (a required field, a date that isn't one). [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/sheets)

- **I made a mistake with a bulk change**: **More → Batch history** in the sidebar → **Undo**. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/undo-and-history)

- **I forgot my password**: Ask an admin: **Manage users** resets it. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/people-and-guests)

- **Rows were skipped on import**: The preview lists each one by its row number in Excel and says why. Fix those rows and import just them: importing the whole sheet again would add the other rows a second time. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/bring-your-lab-in)

- **A colleague's database isn't in my sidebar**: It may be their personal one (*Just you* on its tile), which only they and admins see, or an admin may have switched it off. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/any-organism)

- **A database disappeared from the sidebar**: An admin may have switched it off in **Lab setup**; its data is kept, and it comes back when it is switched on. [→ See the page](https://biomanager.org/guide/lab-setup)

- **Something else**: **Help → Send feedback** in the sidebar (see below), or [open an issue](https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/issues) — say which system you use and what you expected to happen.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/troubleshooting

---

## Feedback

Send feedback to your lab's admins from any page, or open it as a GitHub issue for BioManager's makers.

**Send feedback**, under Help in the sidebar, is for something that went wrong, an idea or a question, from the page you're on. It is kept in your lab: its admins are told, read it on the same page and mark it **Done**. To tell BioManager's makers too, **Open as a GitHub issue**: a new issue opens with your text, the page, the version and the browser filled in (not your server's address, nor your name), for you to check and submit. You need a GitHub account.

Admins also find a **Usage report** there: for each of the last eight weeks, how many people changed something and how many changes in each area, and what the lab holds now. Counts only — no names, nothing anyone wrote — and the report is not sent anywhere: copy the text at the bottom into an email, for instance to whoever runs a pilot with your lab. Below it, **Anonymous counts for BioManager's makers** shows the daily message word for word, with **Switch off** ([more](https://biomanager.org/guide/your-data#counts)).

### On GitHub

You can also go straight to BioManager's GitHub page and [open an issue](https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/issues/new/choose): **Something isn't working** or **An idea or something missing**. Leave out names, lab data, passwords and your server's address. If BioManager helps your lab, [a star on GitHub](https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager) helps other labs find it.

Source: https://biomanager.org/guide/feedback

---

Source: https://biomanager.org/deploy-with-ai.md

# Deploying BioManager: a guide for AI assistants

You are helping someone set up **BioManager**, a lab database for animal
colonies, stocks and inventories, as a server for their lab. This file is
written for you: follow it in order, run the checks, and stop where it says
to ask. The human-readable version is
https://biomanager.org/server.

## Rules

1. **Secrets never pass through the chat.** Passwords, API keys, the
   PostgreSQL password, OAuth client secrets, Backblaze keys, SSH private
   keys: have the person type or paste them directly on the server (in
   `nano .env`, or at a prompt), or generate them there with
   `openssl rand -hex 24`. Do not echo `.env` back into the conversation.
   If you must confirm a value is set, check it is non-empty:
   `grep -c '^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.\+' .env`.
2. **Ask before anything that costs money, can't be undone, or opens the
   server to the internet**: creating cloud resources, upgrading a cloud
   account, buying a domain, opening firewall ports, `internet-access.sh on`,
   restoring a backup, `docker compose down -v` (that deletes the database).
3. **Accounts are theirs.** The person creates cloud, Tailscale, domain and
   OAuth accounts and signs in to them in their own browser. You tell them
   what to click.
4. **Back up before changing a running server:**
   `docker compose exec backup backup.sh`.
5. **Never expose PostgreSQL.** Only Caddy publishes ports (80, 443, and
   8081 on 127.0.0.1 only). Do not add ports to `db` or `app`.
6. After each step, run its **check**. If a check fails, fix that before
   going on; the troubleshooting table below covers the usual causes.

## First, ask

Ask these, then recommend an option (the table after them) and wait for a yes.

1. Who will use it: one person, or a lab (how many people)?
2. Where are they: all in one building on the same network, or also at home,
   on phones on mobile data, or at other sites?
3. Is there a computer that can stay on (and does IT allow running a server
   on the network), or would they rather use a free cloud VM?
4. Do they want an ordinary web address that needs no app (a domain,
   about $10–15 a year), or is installing Tailscale on each device fine?
5. Do they have the desktop app's data already, to move onto the server?
6. Their time zone (for backups and dates).

| Situation | Option |
| --- | --- |
| One person | **A**: the desktop app. No server. Send them to https://biomanager.org/download and stop here. |
| One building, a Linux computer that stays on | **B**: a Linux computer in the lab, `TLS=internal` (or `TLS=files` with IT's certificate). For a Mac, send them to the desktop app: Settings → Set up a lab server → This computer, for the whole lab |
| University offers VMs | **C**: ask IT for a VM with Docker, a DNS name and a certificate; then as B with `TLS=files` |
| People anywhere, most labs | **D**: Ubuntu 24.04 cloud VM + Tailscale, `TLS=tailscale` (recommended; free on Oracle Cloud Always Free) |
| An address that works with no app | **E**: cloud VM + a domain, `TLS=acme`, ports 80/443 open |

## Facts

- **What runs:** four Docker containers from the server bundle: `app`
  (gunicorn, image `ghcr.io/gaspolymerase/biomanager:<version>`), `db`
  (PostgreSQL 16, internal network only), `caddy` (HTTPS), `backup`
  (nightly `pg_dump` + uploads tarball, weekly restore test, optional
  restic off-site).
- **The bundle:**
  `https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/releases/latest/download/biomanager-server.tar.gz`.
  It unpacks to `Biomanager/deploy/`; always unpack it into
  `/opt/biomanager`, so the deploy folder is
  `/opt/biomanager/Biomanager/deploy` (scripts and systemd units assume it).
  `BUNDLE.md`, `README.md` and `RUNBOOK.md` inside are the reference.
- **The app image** is not pulled from a registry: the same release has
  `biomanager-image-amd64.tar.gz` and `biomanager-image-arm64.tar.gz`, and
  `deploy/host/load-image.sh` downloads the one for this machine (for the
  version in `deploy/VERSION`) and `docker load`s it with the tag
  `compose.yaml` expects. Run it after every unpack, before `docker compose up`.
  Check: `docker image ls ghcr.io/gaspolymerase/biomanager` shows the version.
- **Settings:** `deploy/.env` (from `.env.example`, mode 600). Required:
  `DOMAIN`, `TLS` (`internal` | `tailscale` | `acme` | `files`),
  `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` (letters and digits only). Usual: `TZ`,
  `BACKUP_DIR=/opt/biomanager/backups`, `BACKUP_TIME=02:30`, `KEEP_LOCAL=30`.
  With `TLS=tailscale` also `COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yaml:compose.tailscale.yaml`.
  With `TLS=acme` also `ACME_EMAIL`. Optional: `RESTIC_*`/`AWS_*` (off-site,
  set by `host/offsite-setup.sh`), `HEALTHCHECK_PING_URL`,
  `BIOMANAGER_GOOGLE_*`/`BIOMANAGER_MICROSOFT_*` (sign-in), `BIOMANAGER_OIDC_*` (the
  institution's own sign-in, OpenID Connect) or `BIOMANAGER_CILOGON_*` (a SAML-only
  university, through CILogon), SMTP, `BIOMANAGER_TELEMETRY=0` (never send
  BioManager's makers the anonymous daily counts; ask the admin, who can
  also switch them off on the Usage report).
- **First account:** the app prints a one-time setup code in its log; the
  first account created at `https://DOMAIN/register` with it is the admin.
  Later sign-ups wait for an admin's approval.
- **Resources:** 2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk is plenty. ARM (Oracle Ampere)
  and x86-64 both work.
- **Host extras (Linux with systemd):** `sudo host/install.sh` (from the
  deploy folder) installs a watchdog (every 5 min: site, containers, disk, backups) and
  weekly image updates, alerting to an ntfy topic it prints.
  `host/offsite-setup.sh` sets up encrypted off-site backups (asks for the
  key itself). `host/internet-access.sh on|off|status` opens temporary guest
  access via Tailscale Funnel (option D only).

## Option D: cloud VM + Tailscale (recommended)

**D1. Accounts (the person does these).** Oracle Cloud (free tier; home
region can't be changed later) and Tailscale. Ask them to download the
bundle to their own computer too, and open
`Biomanager/deploy/cloud-init.yaml`.

**D2. The VM (the person clicks; you guide).** Compute → Instances →
Create: Ubuntu 24.04; shape VM.Standard.A1.Flex (2 OCPU/12 GB or 4/24); a
public subnet with a public IPv4; their SSH public key (help them run
`ssh-keygen -t ed25519` if they have none; only the `.pub` goes to Oracle);
Advanced → Management → Initialization script: the contents of
`cloud-init.yaml`. "Out of capacity" means try again later or another
availability domain. Any other provider's Ubuntu 24.04 VM works the same;
then run the steps of `cloud-init.yaml`'s `runcmd` by hand if it has no
cloud-init box.

**D3. Tailscale.**

```bash
ssh ubuntu@<public IP>
test -f /var/lib/biomanager-ready && echo ready    # wait for cloud-init
sudo tailscale up --hostname=biomanager            # the person opens the printed link
```

The person, in the Tailscale admin console: Machines → biomanager →
Disable key expiry; DNS → enable MagicDNS and HTTPS Certificates. Ask them
for the tailnet name (`tailXXXX.ts.net`); it is not secret.
Check: `tailscale status` lists the machine; from their computer, with
Tailscale on, `ssh ubuntu@biomanager` works. Continue over that connection
(a fresh login also puts `ubuntu` in the `docker` group cloud-init added it to).

**D4. BioManager.**

```bash
curl -fsSL -o /tmp/biomanager-server.tar.gz \
  https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/releases/latest/download/biomanager-server.tar.gz
tar -xzf /tmp/biomanager-server.tar.gz -C /opt/biomanager
cd /opt/biomanager/Biomanager/deploy
host/load-image.sh
cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env
sed -i "s|^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.*|POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 24)|" .env
sed -i "s|^TLS=.*|TLS=tailscale|; s|^#COMPOSE_FILE=|COMPOSE_FILE=|; s|^BACKUP_DIR=.*|BACKUP_DIR=/opt/biomanager/backups|" .env
sed -i "s|^DOMAIN=.*|DOMAIN=biomanager.tailXXXX.ts.net|; s|^TZ=.*|TZ=<their time zone>|" .env
grep -E '^(DOMAIN|TLS|COMPOSE_FILE|TZ|BACKUP_DIR)=' .env
docker compose config --quiet && echo "settings ok"
docker compose up -d --build
```

Check: `docker compose ps` shows `db` and `app` healthy within a minute or
two, and `backup` healthy once its first backup is done (`health: starting`
until then); `curl -fsS https://biomanager.tailXXXX.ts.net/healthz` prints `ok`;
`docker compose exec backup ls /backups/db` lists a first dump.
Then `docker compose logs app | grep "setup code"`: the person opens
`https://DOMAIN/register` on a device with Tailscale and creates the admin
account with it. The code is single-use; it is fine to show it to them.

**D5. Host extras.** `sudo host/install.sh` (in the deploy folder); tell them to subscribe
to the printed ntfy topic in the ntfy app. Check:
`systemctl list-timers 'biomanager-*'`.

**D6. Close the door (ask first).** In Oracle Cloud, delete the security
list's ingress rule for port 22. Check from their computer:
`ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 ubuntu@<public IP>` times out, while
`ssh ubuntu@biomanager` keeps working over Tailscale.

**D6b. Oracle's idle stop (optional; ask first).** Oracle stops an Always
Free VM that looks idle for a week (starting it again loses nothing).
Upgrading the account to Pay As You Go (Billing) stops that and still bills
nothing for Always Free resources.

**D7. Off-site backups (recommended; ask first).** The person creates a
Backblaze B2 bucket (private, encryption on, Object Lock on with a 30-day
Governance default) and an application key limited to that bucket. Then,
in their own terminal (the script asks for the key and shows the backup
password once, to save in their password manager):
`ssh -t biomanager sudo /opt/biomanager/Biomanager/deploy/host/offsite-setup.sh`.

**D8. The lab.** Members install Tailscale; the person either invites them
to the tailnet or shares the one machine with their own Tailscale accounts
(Machines → biomanager → Share). Members sign up at the address; the admin
approves them in Settings → Manage users. Phones: Android app (download page), or on
iPhone Safari → Share → Add to Home Screen.

## Options B and C: a Linux computer or a university VM

As D4 with `TLS=internal` (B; or `TLS=files` for C, with IT's certificate
and key copied to `deploy/certs/server.crt` and `deploy/certs/server.key`),
`DOMAIN` = a fixed IP or a DNS name that never changes, and no
`COMPOSE_FILE`. Docker: `curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sudo sh`
(then `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER` and log in again); turn off sleep.
By hand this is Linux only (the scripts, timers and `/opt` paths assume
it); on a Mac, the desktop app's Settings → Set up a lab server → This
computer, for the whole lab does it. Create `/opt/biomanager` owned by the
user first:
`sudo mkdir -p /opt/biomanager && sudo chown "$USER" /opt/biomanager`.
With `TLS=internal`, every device must trust Caddy's root once:
`docker compose exec caddy cat /data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt > biomanager-root.crt`,
then install it (macOS Keychain "Always Trust"; Windows "Trusted Root
Certification Authorities"; iOS profile + Certificate Trust Settings;
Android "CA certificate"). Docker publishes 80 and 443 on the machine
itself; a network firewall run by IT must let 443 through from the lab
network (and the VPN). Put `BACKUP_DIR` on a second disk if there is one.

## Option E: a domain

As D, but: a DNS A record `biomanager.<domain>` → the VM's public IP;
inbound TCP 80 and 443 allowed in the cloud firewall (ask first); `.env`
with `DOMAIN=biomanager.<domain>`, `TLS=acme`, `ACME_EMAIL=<their email>`,
no `COMPOSE_FILE`. On Cloudflare DNS, the record must be "DNS only", not
proxied. Check: `docker compose logs caddy | grep "certificate obtained"`
shows `certificate obtained successfully`; `curl -fsS https://biomanager.<domain>/healthz`
from anywhere prints `ok`. Recommend Google or Microsoft sign-in
(`deploy/README.md`, "Signing in with Google or Microsoft") and strong
passwords, since the sign-in page is public.

Cloudflare Tunnel (not packaged; only if they ask): `cloudflared` on the
host pointing at `https://localhost:443` with `originServerName: <DOMAIN>`
(or `noTLSVerify: true` with `TLS=internal`), and Cloudflare Access in
front. Then no inbound ports are needed.

## Moving the desktop app's data in

Only into a **new, empty** server, before its first `docker compose up`
(after `host/load-image.sh` and with `.env` filled in). The app's folder:
macOS `~/Library/Application Support/Biomanager/`, Windows
`%APPDATA%\Biomanager\`, Linux `~/.local/share/Biomanager/`. The database
is `data/biomanager.db` inside it, and the uploaded files are `uploads/`.
The person quits the app and copies both to the server, e.g. from a Mac:

```bash
scp "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Biomanager/data/biomanager.db" <user>@<server>:/tmp/lab.db
scp -r "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Biomanager/uploads" <user>@<server>:/tmp/lab-uploads
```

Then, on the server in the deploy folder:

```bash
docker compose up -d db
docker compose run --rm --no-deps -v /tmp/lab.db:/import/lab.db:ro app \
  sh -c 'python scripts/migrate-to-postgres.py --dry-run /import/lab.db "$DATABASE_URL"'
# if the dry run is clean, the same without --dry-run, then:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose cp /tmp/lab-uploads/. app:/data/uploads/
```

Check: the person signs in with their existing account (no setup code: the
accounts came along) and sees their data. Then D5 (host extras).

## Updating a running server

```bash
cd /opt/biomanager/Biomanager/deploy
docker compose exec backup backup.sh
curl -fsSL -o /tmp/b.tar.gz https://github.com/gaspolymerase/biomanager/releases/latest/download/biomanager-server.tar.gz
tar -xzf /tmp/b.tar.gz -C /opt/biomanager      # .env and backups are not in the bundle
host/load-image.sh && docker compose up -d --build
```

Check: `docker compose ps` healthy; `curl -fsS https://DOMAIN/healthz`
prints `ok`. The database schema updates itself on start; the log then says
`Upgrading the database from … to …`. If it goes wrong: RUNBOOK.md,
"Updating went wrong".

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| `permission denied` on the Docker socket | The user isn't in the `docker` group yet: log out and in, or `newgrp docker` |
| `set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env` / `set DOMAIN in .env` | `.env` is missing that value: run the `sed` lines of D4 again, then `docker compose config --quiet` |
| `pull access denied for ghcr.io/gaspolymerase/biomanager` | The image wasn't loaded: run `host/load-image.sh` in the deploy folder, then `docker compose up -d` |
| `app` never healthy | `docker compose logs app`. A malformed `DATABASE_URL` usually means `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` has symbols: use hex only, then `docker compose down` (not `-v`) and `up -d` |
| `/healthz` fails but containers are healthy | `docker compose logs caddy`. `TLS=tailscale`: HTTPS Certificates not enabled in the tailnet, or `COMPOSE_FILE` missing. `TLS=acme`: DNS not pointing at the VM yet, or port 80 closed |
| Browser says the certificate isn't trusted (`TLS=internal`) | Install `biomanager-root.crt` on that device |
| No setup code in the log | An account already exists; the code is only for the first one. `docker compose logs app \| grep -i "setup"` |
| Oracle: "Out of host capacity" | Try later, another availability domain, or a smaller shape |
| A VM on Oracle's free tier stopped after days idle | Oracle stops Always Free VMs that look idle for a week: start it again in Compute → Instances (nothing is lost). Upgrading the account to Pay As You Go prevents it and still bills nothing for Always Free resources |
| Phones can't reach it | Tailscale off on the phone (D), not on the lab network (B), or the root certificate not installed (`TLS=internal`) |

## When you are done

Tell the person, in plain words: the address; that the first account is the
admin; where backups are (`/opt/biomanager/backups`, nightly, restore-tested
weekly) and whether off-site is on; the ntfy topic for alerts; how to update
(above); and that `deploy/RUNBOOK.md` in the bundle says what to do when an
alert arrives. Fill in its table at the top (*Where everything is*) with them:
the address, the server and where to start or rebuild it, where backups go,
off-site or not, the ntfy topic; and have them keep a copy somewhere other
than the server. The user guide is https://biomanager.org/guide.
